title: Clare
hook: Francis's friend who founded the Poor Clares and, tradition says, faced down soldiers holding the sacrament

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis greeted the end with one word: welcome. Your line was sister death. What ending did you say thank you for? Day eight hundred eighteen.

Soldiers are coming over the wall of a small convent outside Assisi. Inside are women with no weapons. Their abbess is sick in bed. And here's what the old account says she does. She has herself carried to the door. She asks for the sacrament, the consecrated bread, kept in a small box, to be brought and set in front of her. She bows down before it and prays. And the soldiers, the story says, turn back and leave. The woman at the door is Clare, Francis's friend, the one whose sisters came to be called the Poor Clares. Today's word is her name, and the way she met them.

Clare grew up in a noble family in Assisi, the same town as Francis. She heard him preach, and she wanted the life he was living: poor, simple, given to God. The Legend of Saint Clare says she slipped out of her family's house at night and went to Francis and his brothers, who cut her hair as a sign she was leaving the old life behind. When her relatives came to drag her home, she held onto the altar and showed them her shorn head, and they let her be. She settled at a little church called San Damiano, and other women came. One of them was her own sister. Their life was enclosed, prayerful and poor, and Clare held onto that poverty for years, asking church leaders to let her sisters own nothing at all. Back to the door. In some tellings, as she prays before the sacrament, a voice answers that God will always guard them. Whatever you make of the story, it says something about Clare: her defense was not a wall or a sword, but stillness and prayer before what she held most holy. Catholics and other Christians honor her as a saint. And the same Legend tells of her last days. Lying ill, she speaks to her own soul. Go forth in peace, she says, for you will have a good escort. The woman who walked out of her father's house at night ends by sending her soul out the door, without fear.
screen: `OUT OF HER FATHER'S HOUSE AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand calmly in a doorway. Any door will do, the bedroom, the kitchen, the front door. Stand in the frame, feet on the floor, hands loose. Breathe. Notice what comes through doorways in your life: news, people, worry. Don't block it and don't rush out to meet it. Just stand there, steady. If you pray, you can hold someone in mind who is facing something frightening today. If you don't, just let the breath be slow, and let the doorway hold you up. The bell holds the time.
Clare. Francis's friend, who left home at night for a poor life, led the sisters at San Damiano, and, the story says, met soldiers at the door with prayer.
Your line: go forth in peace. Each time you walk out a door today, say it under your breath, to yourself or to the person leaving with you. Day eight hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: The Poor Clares live an enclosed life of prayer in convents around the world, and Catholics and some Anglicans keep a feast day for Saint Clare.

notes: All Clare narrative is paraphrased from the Legend of Saint Clare; confirm each beat (night flight, hair cut at the Portiuncula, clinging to the altar, the attack on San Damiano, the voice, her words to her soul). The soldiers' identity (in Frederick II's army) is left out on purpose.

Her last words are given as 'Go forth in peace, for you have followed a good road', to match the index carry. Translations vary ('go forth without fear', 'you have a good escort'); confirm the paraphrase is fair.
'Her own sister' joining her: Agnes of Assisi. Confirm.
'Asking church leaders to let her sisters own nothing at all' refers to the privilege of poverty; no dates given. Confirm.
'Catholics and other Christians honor her as a saint' and howItsDone 'some Anglicans': confirm phrasing under the claims rule.
Index hook says 'founded the Poor Clares'; the script says her sisters 'came to be called the Poor Clares'. Confirm.
Editor: cut the invented 'no locks worth the name'; her last words now follow the sources' 'good escort' rather than 'a good road'; varied the hook's closing line.
Auditor: the Legend has Clare carried to the door and bowing in prayer, not standing; 'the way she stood there' and 'standing still' reworded to match.
